# The Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

There's a particular kind of magic that lives in the unremarkable. Not the obvious magic of sunsets or mountains or waterfalls—though those are magnificent in their way—but the quiet, overlooked magic that exists in the everyday objects and moments we pass without thinking. I want to talk about that for a while, because I think we've collectively underestimated how much beauty and meaning can be found in things we've learned to ignore.

Consider a simple wooden spoon. Most kitchens have several, and most people think nothing of them. They're tools, functional objects, temporary holders of soup or sauce before the food makes its way to mouths. But if you actually look at a wooden spoon—really look at it—there's something rather extraordinary happening. The wood has a grain, patterns created by years of the tree's growth, each line representing weather, seasons, nutrients drawn from soil. Someone shaped this tree into this specific form, wore it smooth through handling. It bears the scars of use: slight darkening from years of heat, maybe a small burn mark where it touched the edge of a pot. It's been held by human hands dozens of times. It's been trusted with food intended to nourish people. And we think nothing of it.

Or consider the experience of walking through a quiet street early in the morning, when most people are still asleep. The light comes at a different angle than it does during the day. It's softer, somehow more honest. You notice things you've never seen before despite walking this street a hundred times: the particular architecture of a building you usually pass in a hurry, the way water collects in a certain spot, what plants grow in which gardens. The absence of the usual crowd of people changes everything. You're not swimming upstream through crowds; you're moving through the space as though the street belongs more fully to you, or perhaps you belong more fully to the street. There's a reciprocal relationship that forms in silence that doesn't exist when you're competing for space and attention.

What strikes me most about these quiet moments and ordinary objects is how much our experience of them depends on our attention. The spoon is always beautiful in the way I described, but you won't notice unless you stop and look. The street is always transforming with the light, but you won't see it unless you slow down. This suggests something important: that a huge portion of what we call "reality" is actually constructed by our attention. The world is always rich and complex and beautiful, but we move through it in a kind of filter mode, paying attention only to what we've decided is important or interesting or relevant to our immediate goals.

I think about this a lot when I notice people, including myself, scrolling through their phones, looking for novelty and excitement and news and entertainment, when all around them there's this immense depth available. Not in a condemning way—I understand why we do this. Our attention is a limited resource, and there's a lot competing for it. The algorithm is designed by very clever people to be addictive. But the opportunity cost is real. For every moment of attention we give to a screen showing us something designed to provoke an emotional reaction, it's a moment we're not available to the actual world around us.

There's a practice in some contemplative traditions called "noting," where you simply observe what's happening without judgment. You notice that you're breathing. You notice that your mind is thinking. You notice that you're sitting. The point isn't to achieve some special state or have a profound experience. It's to develop a kind of clear-eyed awareness of what's actually present. And what's remarkable is how this practice, when done consistently, begins to reveal that the present moment is already profound. You don't need anything special to happen. Just being alive, breathing, thinking, aware—this is already extraordinary if you can see it clearly.

I've been thinking a lot lately about memory and how it shapes our relationship with time. We preserve memories through photographs and journals and videos, trying to hold onto moments that are slipping away even as we live them. There's something beautiful about this impulse—the desire to not forget, to honor the significance of a moment by capturing it. But I wonder if sometimes we've inverted something important. We preserve the moments in order to truly experience them, rather than experiencing the moments in order to naturally preserve what matters in memory. The camera becomes a barrier between us and the event rather than a tool.

I spent time recently watching my grandmother's hands while she was doing ordinary tasks—washing dishes, folding laundry, peeling vegetables. Her hands are old now, marked with age spots and wrinkles and the accumulated evidence of eighty-five years of living. They move with a kind of efficiency and grace, and there's information encoded in them: everything she's done, everywhere she's touched, everything she's made. I thought about how these hands held my mother when my mother was born, held me when I was born, have fed people throughout her life, have created and mended and built. And I realized that if I had only been taking photographs of this moment, I would have missed the actual experience of witnessing those hands, of understanding something about continuity and mortality and love that no photograph could convey.

There's a literary term called "defamiliarization," which describes the technique of making the familiar seem strange in order to make us see it fresh. Authors do this by describing ordinary things in unusual ways or from unusual perspectives. The purpose is to wake us up from our automatic way of perceiving. It's a way of saying: you think you know what this is, but look again, really look. I think we need more of this in our daily life. Not in a forced or artificial way, but naturally, as a practice. The defamiliarization that happens when you look at something ordinary with full attention.

I've noticed that certain times of year trigger this for me naturally. Autumn does it most. Suddenly the trees are doing something dramatic, the light is changing noticeably day by day, the weather is shifting. It's impossible to ignore because the change is so visible. Spring does it too, though in a different way—everything is aggressively growing and changing and beginning. But winter and summer, once we've settled into them, can feel static. The days don't seem to change much. The same temperature, the same light pattern, the same everything. And yet of course they're changing constantly. It's just slower, more subtle. A practice that appeals to me is trying to notice the subtle changes in the seasons when they're not dramatic. What's different about today compared to yesterday? What's growing that wasn't there last week? What's wilting? What insects are present now that weren't a month ago?

This connects to something I think about regarding meaning. We tend to look for meaning in big moments—graduations, weddings, deaths, moves, achievements. But I suspect that meaning is actually distributed throughout our lives more evenly than we realize. The fact that you're able to perceive anything at all is miraculous. That your brain is doing something so complex that you're able to read these words and understand them—this is not less miraculous because it happens every day. If anything, it's more miraculous because of how it survives being ordinary.

There's a philosopher I think about named Ludwig Wittgenstein, who spent some of his later life working as a gardener and a teacher in a village. After decades of abstract philosophical work, he seemed to find something important in this simple work, in paying attention to things as they are rather than as we theorize they should be. He talked about the importance of "describing the landscape" rather than imposing patterns on it. I think that's part of what I'm trying to get at. How do we develop the capacity to see what's actually there, before we've categorized it and filed it and decided whether we care about it?

One more observation: I've found that my capacity to find beauty and meaning in ordinary things is directly correlated with my mental and emotional state. When I'm depressed or anxious, the world flattens out. Everything feels gray and routine, even things that usually interest me. The spoon is just a spoon. The early morning street is just an empty street. But when I'm healthier in my mind, the same things glow with significance. This suggests to me that meaning isn't entirely objective, inscribed in the world waiting to be discovered. It's also something we create through our engagement with the world, through our willingness to be present and open.

This is hopeful to me, actually. It means that if we want to experience more beauty and meaning, we have some agency in that. We can practice presence. We can slow down. We can look at ordinary things with curiosity. We can resist the constant pull toward novelty and stimulation. We can take seriously the idea that right here, in this moment, there's probably something worth noticing.

I'll end with something simple: tomorrow, pick something you usually ignore. A door handle. A houseplant. A sidewalk. A piece of clothing you wear regularly. Stop and really look at it for a minute or two. Notice its texture, its color, how light plays on it, how it came to be. Notice how your attention works. Notice if it changes how you feel. You might be surprised. Or you might find nothing special about it at all. And that's fine too. But you might also discover that the world around you is even richer than you remembered.
